title: The Truth About Fiction
author: Colton Cauthen
summary: Colton Cauthen recounts how he came to reading as an adult through nonfiction alone, dismissing novels as a lesser use of time, until G.K. Chesterton's Orthodoxy and The Story of the Family upended that assumption. The essay argues that a common bias -- nonfiction is for growth, fiction is for entertainment -- rests on a flawed reduction of growth to mere factual knowledge. Leaning on Peter Kreeft's account of the soul's three 'prophets' (intellect, imagination, conscience) and their corresponding goods (truth, beauty, goodness), Cauthen contends that nonfiction largely serves the intellect alone while fiction also forms the imagination and conscience. He invokes Chesterton's claim that the novel is 'more true' than science or metaphysics because life itself is always experienced as a story, and argues that fiction preserves the wholeness of human experience that analytical nonfiction necessarily breaks into parts. The piece closes with a Great Books-flavored appeal: readers should include serious fiction (Dostoevsky, Shelley, Orwell, Huxley) alongside nonfiction to avoid becoming, in C.S. Lewis's phrase, 'men without chests.'
points: Cauthen traces his shift from an adult 'nonfiction-only' reading habit to embracing fiction back to G.K. Chesterton, arguing that growth requires more than the accumulation of facts.
Drawing on Peter Kreeft's three 'prophets' of the soul (intellect, imagination, conscience), the piece argues nonfiction speaks mainly to truth while fiction also reaches beauty and goodness.

Citing Chesterton's claim that 'the novel is more true' than science or metaphysics, the essay argues good fiction captures the wholeness of lived experience that analytical nonfiction necessarily fragments.
Fiction is framed as both culture-expressing and culture-shaping (Uncle Tom's Cabin, The Jungle, the Odyssey) -- novels don't just reflect a society's values, they help form them.

The essay's C.S. Lewis-inflected close on 'men without chests' positions fiction as necessary for forming sentiment and conviction, not just intellect, making a Great Books case against a purely utilitarian reading diet.
quotes: The core problem with this assumption is that it reduces growth to knowledge and limits knowledge to a particular type of knowledge. Having restricted growth to increasing one's knowledge, it then flattens knowledge to mean only technical information; the assimilation of new data; the storing of facts -- all things nonfiction works are generally designed to help us do.

The Philosopher Peter Kreeft suggests that the human soul has three prophets: the intellect, the imagination, and the conscience. These prophets reveal to us three aspects of reality: truth, beauty, and goodness, respectively. Nonfiction generally appeals only, or at least primarily, to the first of these: to propositional truths, understood as external facts.

One of the reasons fiction is indispensable to the serious reader is that it makes up a substantial part of the culture-expressing and culture-shaping body of literature. Works of fiction are a gateway into understanding culture -- whether that of others, or your own.

Speaking in great generality, nonfiction is adept at filling and forming the head (the rational; the intellectual), while fiction is adept at forming the chest (the sentiments, the orientation, the conviction). If we wish to avoid men without chests or bodies without heads, it's a good idea to include both fiction and nonfiction in our diet.

People wonder why the novel is the most popular form of literature; people wonder why it is read more than books of science or books of metaphysics. The reason is very simple; it is merely that the novel is more true than they are.
Fiction stands as something of a bulwark against this trend by preserving that wholeness and presenting it to us in a complete story. And stories are powerful -- they move us and help us remember.
